Euphausia superba, the Antarctic krill, exhibits a life history finely tuned to the extreme seasonality of the Southern Ocean. The species commences development from a subitaneous egg with an initial wet weight of approximately 65 micrograms [Ww0 = approximately 65 micrograms], a value computed from an egg diameter of 0.5 millimeters under the assumption of a specific density of 1 gram per cubic centimeter. Upon hatching, the lecithotrophic nauplius emerges; the age at hatch is approximately 6 days  when development occurs at 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C]. The yolk-sac larva is entirely reliant on endogenous reserves during this period. This developmental pathway leads to the free-swimming calyptopis stage, a critical transition that marks the onset of exogenous feeding and the beginning of active growth in the water column. At this onset of external feeding, the wet weight at birth is recorded as 0.125 milligrams [Wwb = 0.125 milligrams]. The progression through these early life stages is notably rapid, enabling the species to exploit the brief, productive summer bloom for juvenile development.

The metamorphosis from the calyptopis to the furcilia stage constitutes a pivotal morphological and ecological shift in the life cycle of Euphausia superba. This transformation is achieved when the juvenile crustacean attains a total length at metam of 1.1 centimeters . The time since birth at this metamorphic event is 32 days  when development occurs under the stable thermal conditions of 0 °C [T = 0 °C]. Measurements from developmental studies indicate that the wet weight at this critical stage is recorded as 2.700 milligrams , marking the transition from a fully lecithotrophic existence to an actively filtering, exotrophic lifestyle. This milestone is strongly temperature-dependent, with the duration of the naupliar and calyptopis phases collectively constraining the timing of metamorphosis. The ability to reach the furcilia stage before the end of the austral summer is essential for accumulating sufficient lipid reserves to survive the subsequent winter period of low food availability.

Sexual maturation in Euphausia superba is a process contingent upon both size and seasonal cues, and the onset of reproductive maturity is marked by the attainment of a total length at puberty of 3.5 centimeters [Lp = 3.5 centimeters]. At this developmental threshold, the wet weight at puberty for an individual is estimated to be 0.590 grams [Wwp = 0.590 grams]. The time since hatch required to reach this pubertal stage is 365 days [tp = 365 days] when krill are reared under a thermal regime of 3 °C [T = 3 °C]. This age at puberty corresponds roughly to the end of the first year of life, a pattern that aligns with the onset of the first spawning season in the field. The capacity to achieve this size threshold is heavily influenced by the duration and intensity of the summer phytoplankton bloom, with interannual variability in food supply leading to substantial differences in the proportion of the cohort that matures in any given year.

The ultimate size and longevity of Euphausia superba are key parameters defining its demographic structure and its role in the Southern Ocean food web. The maximum recorded total length, or ultimate total length, for the species is 6.1 centimeters [Li = 6.1 centimeters], a size that corresponds to an asymptotic wet weight of 3.654 grams [Wwi = 3.654 grams]. This adult body mass represents the culmination of somatic growth, after which energy is primarily directed toward reproductive effort. The lifespan of this species is considerable for a small crustacean, with a maximum longevity of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] when maintained under the stable, cold conditions of 2 °C [T = 2 °C]. This relatively long lifespan, combined with iteroparous reproduction, allows the population to buffer against years of poor recruitment. Such a life-history strategy is common among high-latitude zooplankton that must contend with extended periods of food scarcity. The age at birth, defined as the time from spawning to the release of the free-swimming nauplius, has a duration of 31 days [ab = 31 days] at 0 °C [T = 0 °C].

Each spawning event by a single female typically yields a large number of eggs, with reported values often exceeding several thousand per clutch. The frequency of these reproductive events, however, is constrained by the brief window of high primary productivity, and most field data indicate that females produce only a single brood each year. The timing of this annual spawning event is tightly coupled with the spring phytoplankton bloom, ensuring that the first feeding larval stages encounter adequate food concentrations. This reproductive strategy, characterized by high per-event fecundity but a low annual frequency, is typical of a capital breeder that must rely on accumulated energy reserves to fuel egg production. The consequence of this pattern is that population recruitment is highly sensitive to the duration and magnitude of the summer productive season.
